title: Week 1 Overview: Integrating Fashion Data
text: I'm Ashasvi Rachel, and this is week one of Causal Couture, a four-part progress series for humanitarians AI. This week was about integration, bringing the project's earlier data architecture and analytical components together into a functioning end-to-end prototype. The starting point was four separate categories of fashion business data, sales, inventory, social engagement, and web activity. Each

title: The Four Core Data Sources: Sales, Inventory, Social, and Web
text: Represented a different part of the business. Week one began by bringing those sources into one analytical workflow. The first step was integrating those four source data sets. text: Provided the inputs for the prototype. Integration alone was not enough. The ingestion and preprocessing workflow also had to standardize the sources and prepare them for downstream analysis. That created a consistent path from incoming data through validation and preprocessing without assuming that the original sources already shared one

title: Designing the Feature Layer & Heuristic Business Scorecard
text: Structure. After preprocessing, the sources were combined into a unified analytical data set at the date by SKU level. That common grain connected different business signals around the same product and date, giving the analytical layer one consistent foundation. From that unified data set, I began building the decision support feature layer. One group represented sales and demand activity. Another captured inventory availability and low stock conditions.

title: The Tech Stack: FastAPI, Polars, and DuckDB
text: These features described pressure on demand and possible risk on the stock side. The feature layer also included social engagement and web conversion behavior, along with sales and social spikes, sell-through behavior, and view-to-cart conversion. At this stage, these were analytical signals derived from the integrated data, not causal effects and not forecasts. Those features supported the phase three heuristic business scorecard. The scorecard organized the

title: Establishing the Methodological Boundary
text: Available information into four primary signals, demand pressure, stock risk, engagement momentum, and conversion strength. The four signals were then combined into an overall score and a rule-based recommendation. The purpose was to translate several analytical signals into an output that could be easier to interpret as business decision support. The next step was connecting the analytical workflow to an interactive front end. Python and fast API provided the API layer. The data processing workflow used tools including pandas, polars, CSV and parquet data structures, and duck DB related architecture. By the end of the week, the broader workflow could move from source data through validation and pre-processing into the unified data set, then through the analytical scorecard and

Recommendation layer, and finally to the interactive front end. But the methodological boundary matters. These phase three scores were heuristic decision support signals. They were not causal estimates and they were not demand forecasts. The prototype could organize and summarize the available signals, but it could not establish cause and effect or predict future demand. The week one output was a working phase three end-to-end analytical prototype. Four source categories, one unified analytical data set, a business signal scorecard, a rule-based recommendation layer, an API, and an interactive front end. Next, extending the prototype into the next analytical phase. This was causal couture, week one of four. I'm Ash as we Rachel documenting the project's progress for Humanitarian's AI.
